olivia.text:
Olivia's chart tells a less obvious story than its current #1 ranking suggests. Births actually peaked in 2014 at 19,836 and have fallen 26% over the past decade, down to 14,718 in 2024. It holds the top spot not because it's still climbing but because names in general have spread across a wider field of choices, so the #1 name today needs a smaller share of the total than it did a generation ago.

Olivia has been given to American girls in every decade since the SSA started counting in 1880, which is unusual longevity for a name with no single film, show, or celebrity tied to its rise. Judi Dench, Olivia de Havilland, and Olivia Rodrigo are all connected to the name but from different eras and different fields entirely, which is more likely a symptom of the name's staying power than a cause of it.

The practical case for Olivia hasn't really changed: three syllables that read as formal on paper, a soft opening sound, and a built-in nickname (Liv, Ollie) for parents who want options later. That combination of stability and flexibility is probably why it's held the #1 rank since 2019 even as the raw count declines.

liam.text:
Liam is currently in the unusual position of being both the most popular boy's name in America and still growing — 22,164 births in 2024, its highest count ever, up 20% over the past decade. That's a different shape than most names at the top of the chart, which tend to be sliding down from an earlier peak even while holding rank.

The name barely existed as a US birth record before the late 1940s and didn't take off until decades later, originally as the Irish short form of William before becoming a name in its own right. It's held the #1 spot continuously since 2017, which is a long run by modern standards, when turnover at the top used to happen every few years.

Its famous bearers skew recent and specific — Liam Payne, Liam Hemsworth, Formula One's Liam Lawson — which suggests the name's rise tracks a generation of parents naming after people roughly their own age rather than historical figures, a pattern that's less common among older top-ranked names like James or William.

noah.text:
Noah has held a top-two US ranking almost continuously since 2013, and its 2024 count of 20,337 is close to its all-time high, up a modest 5% over the past decade — a slower climb than Liam's but a steadier one, without the swings that hit most biblical names in recent decades.

What sets Noah apart from most names this popular is its span: it appears in SSA records going all the way back to 1880, present in every decade since, long before its recent surge. That kind of continuous low-level use before a breakout is rare among current top-10 names, most of which were essentially absent before the 1980s or 1990s.

The famous-bearer list is unusually varied for a name this size — a historian (Yuval Noah Harari), a 18th-century lexicographer (Noah Webster), a Grammy-winning musician (Adam Levine), and a sprinter (Noah Lyles) — spanning centuries and fields rather than clustering around one recent cultural moment, which tracks with a name whose popularity was already broad before it became the biggest name in the country.

oliver.text:
Oliver's 2024 count of 15,343 is its highest ever and represents 62% growth over the past decade, the strongest ten-year gain of any name in the current US top five. It first cracked the top three in 2019 and has held there since, a rapid rise for a name that spent most of the 20th century well outside the top 50.

The name has been in continuous use since 1880, giving it a longer paper trail than its recent popularity might suggest. Its most prominent historical bearer, Oliver Cromwell, sits at the opposite end of the name's public image from its current soft, storybook-adjacent appeal — a reminder that a name's associations can shift entirely across four centuries of use.

Oliver's growth has tracked closely with Liam's and Noah's rather than following its own separate trend, all three -er/-ah ending names rising together through the 2010s and 2020s. That kind of clustered movement, several similar-sounding names climbing in parallel, is more typical of a broader sound preference than any one name's individual appeal.

emma.text:
Emma is the clearest case among the current top names of a peak already passed: it topped the chart at 22,719 births in 2003 and held #1 through 2008, but 2024's count of 13,485 is down 36% from a decade ago, even though it still ranks #2 nationally.

That gap between rank and raw count is the real story here. Emma's own numbers make the point: it needed 22,719 births to be the #1 name in 2003, but today's #2 spot only takes 13,485, well under two-thirds of that — because parents are drawing from a much wider pool of choices than they were twenty years ago. Emma isn't fading so much as the whole naming landscape has spread out underneath it.

The name has been recorded every year since 1880, and its famous bearers — Jane Austen's Emma predates the data, but Emma Watson, Emma Thompson, and Emma Goldman span acting and activism across more than a century — suggest a name that's been quietly available the whole time, waiting for its turn rather than arriving with any single moment.

amelia.text:
Amelia's birth count peaked in 2021 at 13,032, and its rank reached its own best-ever mark, #3, in 2024 — essentially where it sits now. That's a 45% rise over the past decade, one of the few names in the current top ten still gaining rather than sliding from an earlier high.

Unlike most names in this range, the enrichment data doesn't attach it to a clear linguistic origin, and its most prominent historical namesake, Empress Amélie of Brazil, is a specific royal figure rather than a broad cultural reference point most parents would recognize today. That makes Amelia's rise harder to pin on any single influence.

What the data does show is a name gaining altitude at exactly the moment several -a-ending names (Olivia, Sophia, Isabella) are declining from their own earlier peaks — Amelia's climb looks less like an isolated trend and more like it's catching some of the demand that those names are shedding as parents look for something with a similar sound but less market saturation.

charlotte.text:
Charlotte reached its highest-ever count in 2021 at 13,362 births and has eased only slightly since, to 12,552 in 2024 — a 24% rise over the decade despite dropping one rank position from its 2021 peak of #3 to #4 today, which points to a name holding steady while others around it move faster.

It's been in the SSA data continuously since 1880, but its modern rise is recent and sharp: the name spent most of the 20th century well below its current position before climbing through the 2010s. Princess Charlotte of Wales, born 2015, sits right at the start of that acceleration, though the name was already well into its ascent by then.

The literary association — Charlotte Brontë — gives the name a different kind of cultural weight than most current top-ten names carry, less tied to any specific celebrity generation and more to a centuries-old reference point, which may partly explain why its growth has been gradual rather than a sudden spike.

mia.text:
Mia is a smaller name than its #5 ranking suggests — 12,113 births in 2024, its highest count since the name first peaked at 14,939 in 2015. The current figure marks a new high in rank even as the raw count sits below the 2015 peak, another example of the top of the chart getting less crowded rather than any one name surging.

The name entered SSA records later than most on this list, first appearing in 1933, and its rise has been comparatively recent and fast for something now sitting in the top five. A 10% decline over the past decade suggests it's past its steepest growth phase even while still gaining rank.

Its famous bearers cut across sport, science, and politics — soccer's Mia Hamm, astrophysicist Andrea M. Ghez, Barbadian prime minister Mia Mottley — rather than clustering in entertainment the way many short, punchy names' namesake lists tend to, which may reflect that Mia works as a standalone name in several languages rather than as a nickname import.

sophia.text:
Sophia's trajectory is one of the sharper reversals in the current top ten: it was the #1 girls' name as recently as 2011, peaking at 22,335 births in 2012, and now sits at #6 with 12,088 in 2024 — a 35% drop over just the past decade, among the sharper reversals in this batch though not the sharpest.

It's been recorded since 1880, giving it more than a century of continuous use before its 2010s surge, and the name carries genuine historical range: Sophia of Hanover was an actual 17th-century royal, distinct from more recently invented "sophia" variants used in branding or fiction.

The decline pattern here looks similar to Emma's and Isabella's — all three peaked in the early-to-mid 2010s and have fallen by roughly a third since — suggesting a cohort of once-dominant, classically-toned names that rose together and are now cooling together, likely displaced by shorter or less familiar alternatives among parents looking for something that reads as less common.

theodore.text:
Theodore's 2024 count of 12,011 is its highest ever, and the 272% rise over the past decade is the largest ten-year gain of any name in this batch by a wide margin — a genuine breakout rather than a gradual climb, going from a niche choice to the #4 boys' name in barely more than ten years.

The name has been present in SSA data since 1880 but spent nearly all of that history well outside the top ranks, making its recent jump unusually steep for a name with no single obvious trigger — no blockbuster character or celebrity baby tied to the surge that the data can confirm.

Its nickname options (Theo, Teddy) likely help explain part of the appeal: a formal, old-fashioned full name that still offers a soft, casual short form, a combination that several other currently rising names (Theodore, Sebastian to a lesser extent) share and that seems to be a stronger predictor of growth right now than the formal name's sound alone.

james.text:
James is the name with by far the longest history in this batch — 5,262,396 total US births since 1880, more than ten times Noah's total. It peaked in 1947 at 94,763 births in a single year, a scale no name reaches today because the pool of names parents choose from is so much wider now.

At 11,793 births in 2024, a comparatively mild 18% below its count a decade earlier, it still holds the #5 national rank — remarkable stability for a name that was already the #1 boys' name in 1940, 84 years earlier.

The famous-bearer list reflects that long history: James Joyce, James Cook, James Madison, James Clerk Maxwell — figures spanning three centuries rather than a recent cultural cluster. Few names carry that kind of multi-generational, multi-field presence while still ranking in the current top five.

henry.text:
Henry's 2024 count of 11,547 is an all-time high for the name, edging past its previous best and landing it at #6 nationally — quietly one of the more durable comebacks in the current top ten, since the name spent much of the mid-20th century well off its 1880s-era standing before climbing back.

It's been recorded in every decade since 1880 and has grown 22% over the past ten years, a steady rather than explosive rise. Unlike Theodore's recent breakout, Henry's climb has been gradual, without a single dramatic jump year.

Its famous bearers lean industrial and intellectual rather than entertainment-driven — Henry Ford, Henry Kissinger, Henry David Thoreau, and, more recently, Bill Gates (born William Henry Gates) — a spread that favors substance over celebrity, which fits a name whose modern revival seems to be about restoring an old-fashioned classic rather than chasing a trend.

mateo.text:
Mateo is the fastest-moving name in this batch relative to its size: a 202% rise over the past decade, second only to Theodore's growth rate, taking it from a niche choice to #7 nationally with 11,302 births in 2024, its highest count on record.

It first appears in SSA data in 1904 but stayed a minor presence for most of the following century, meaning almost all of its current volume has arrived in the last twenty years. That makes Mateo one of the more recent additions to the top ten by total-history standards, alongside Ezra.

Its famous bearers are almost entirely contemporary and international — footballers Mateo Kovačić and Mateo Retegui, both active professionals rather than historical figures — a contrast with names like James or William whose namesake lists stretch back centuries. That skew toward recent, globally visible figures fits a name whose US popularity is itself a recent development tied to broader interest in Spanish-language names.

elijah.text:
Elijah peaked in 2011 at 13,997 births and has fallen 20% over the past decade to 11,171 in 2024, dropping from its best-ever rank of #4 in 2020 to #8 today — a decline that's milder than Sophia's or Isabella's but points the same direction: biblical names that surged in the 2000s and 2010s cooling from their highs.

The name has been in continuous SSA use since 1880, giving it well over a century of quiet presence before its 21st-century rise, similar to Noah's pattern but on a smaller scale and with an earlier peak.

Its famous-bearer list is notably eclectic for a biblical name — actor Elijah Wood, musician Lil Peep, Nation of Islam leader Elijah Muhammad, Olympic swimmer Elijah Winnington — spanning very different public identities rather than reinforcing one image, which may be part of why the name reads as flexible rather than tied to any single association.

isabella.text:
Isabella's fall from #1 is the steepest of any former chart-topper in this batch: it held the top national rank as recently as 2009, peaked at 22,935 births in 2010, and now sits at #7 with 10,770 in 2024 — a 37% decline over the past decade, on par with Sophia's drop and part of the same broader retreat of early-2010s chart-topping names.

It's been recorded since 1880 and, like Sophia, carries real historical range: the enrichment data's oldest reference is Sojourner Truth's birth name, Isabella Baumfree, a very different association from the name's more recent pop-culture ties through nickname variants like Bella.

That nickname flexibility — Bella Hadid and Bella Ramsey both appear in its famous-bearer list under the shortened form — may be cushioning the decline somewhat, since Isabella functions as both a formal choice and, via Bella, a softer one, giving it two separate routes back into favor even as the full name's raw numbers fall.

lucas.text:
Lucas has had one of the more gradual, low-volatility trajectories in this batch: it peaked in 2017 at 13,029 births. Ten years on, 10,703 births in 2024 puts it just 12% below that mark — a smaller pullback than most of its early-2010s-peaking peers like Isabella or Sophia, holding at #9 nationally.

The name dates back to 1881 in SSA records and has been present in every decade since, longer continuous use than several other names currently ranked above it, like Theodore or Mateo, even though it now sits slightly lower on the chart.

Its famous-bearer list includes figures across thirteen centuries of use — Luke the Evangelist's association at one end, contemporary footballers Lucas Vázquez and Lucas Hernández at the other — with Lucas Cranach the Elder's Renaissance-era art in between, a name that has apparently never gone fully out of circulation long enough to become strongly associated with any single era.

william.text:
William's scale dwarfs nearly every other name in this batch: 4,205,026 total US births since 1880, and it held the #2 national rank in 1880 itself, the earliest year in the data — meaning the name was already firmly established well over a century before this dataset begins its count.

Its 1947 peak of 67,001 births in a single year reflects an era when a much smaller set of names covered most babies born. William now ranks #10 with 10,596 births in 2024, 37% below its count from ten years prior, but that has to be read against a name that's simply operating in a far more fragmented naming landscape than it once was.

The famous-bearer list underscores the name's long reach — William Shakespeare, Stephen Hawking, Bertrand Russell — literary and scientific figures spanning five centuries. Few currently top-ten names carry that kind of unbroken historical weight while still ranking among America's most-used names today.

benjamin.text:
Benjamin peaked comparatively long ago for a name still in the current top 15: 15,733 births in 1989. From there it's been a slow, multi-decade slide rather than a recent turn — 9,814 births in 2024, 29% below where it stood ten years earlier.

It's been recorded since 1880, giving it well over a century of steady, largely unspectacular use — never a chart-topper like William or James, but rarely absent from the top tier either, a kind of durability without ever needing a single breakout moment.

Its famous-bearer list is dominated by early American figures — Benjamin Franklin, Benjamin Harrison — reflecting the name's deep roots in US naming culture specifically, distinct from names like Mateo or Theodore whose rises are more recent and less tied to any particular national historical figure.

levi.text:
Levi is a smaller-scale name than most in this batch but a stable one: it peaked in 2022 at 9,861 births and sits at 9,513 in 2024, essentially flat over the past year and up 18% over the full decade — growth without the sharp swings seen in Theodore or Mateo.

The name has been recorded since 1880 and has held a fairly consistent, modest presence through most of that history, only recently climbing into the current top 12 rather than arriving as a sudden new entrant.

Its most commercially famous bearer, Levi Strauss, ties the name to 19th-century American manufacturing rather than entertainment or sport, an unusual anchor point among current top-15 names' famous-bearer lists, most of which lean toward recent actors or athletes like Zachary Levi, who also appears here as a more contemporary reference.

ezra.text:
Ezra had its single best year on record in 2024, with 8,774 births — its current count and its all-time peak are the same number, meaning the name hasn't yet shown any sign of slowing. The 156% rise over the past decade is the third-largest ten-year gain in this batch, behind only Theodore and Mateo.

It's been present in SSA data since 1880 but, like Mateo, stayed a minor presence for most of that span; nearly all of its current volume reflects growth within the last fifteen years, making it one of the more recently arrived names in the current top 15 by historical weight.

The famous-bearer list mixes the biblical scribe Ezra with poet Ezra Pound and actor Ezra Miller, plus musician George Ezra, whose stage name uses it as a surname rather than a given name — a reminder that a name's public visibility doesn't always come from people who were given it at birth.

evelyn.text:
Evelyn's story runs opposite to most names in this batch: it actually peaked back in 1921 at 14,278 births, decades before almost every other name here reached its high point, and has spent the century since well below that level — its 2024 count of 9,116 is still 4% higher than a decade ago, a slow modern recovery rather than a decline from a recent peak.

The name has been recorded every year since 1880, giving it one of the longest and most stable histories in this batch, present through the entire 20th century rather than arriving as a recent addition like Mateo or Ezra.

Its famous-bearer list spans writer Evelyn Waugh, ballerina Margot Fonteyn, and actress Angela Bassett — a name used by both men and women historically (Waugh was male), which may partly explain its unusually long, low-drama presence in the data rather than the sharp peak-and-decline pattern more common among names tied to one specific era or gender association.

ava.text:
Ava peaked in 2007 at 18,053 births and has fallen sharply since, down 45% over the past decade to 8,662 in 2024 — the steepest decline of any name in this batch, dropping from a best-ever rank of #3 in 2016 to #9 today.

It's been in SSA records since 1880 but, like several names in this group, spent most of that history in minor use before a rapid rise beginning in the 2000s — meaning its current decline is really the back half of a fairly short, sharp cycle rather than a long slow fade.

Ava Gardner's mid-20th-century fame predates the name's actual popularity boom by half a century, which suggests the name's recent rise wasn't really about her; its shorter, punchier famous-bearer list (singer Ava Max, director Ava DuVernay) reflects a name whose visible cultural presence caught up with its birth-record popularity only after the fact rather than driving it.

sebastian.text:
Sebastian has moved in a narrow band for nearly a decade: it peaked in 2016 at 10,308 births, held its best-ever rank of #13 in 2022, and sits at 8,562 in 2024, down a modest 8% over the past decade — one of the more stable trajectories in this batch, without a sharp rise or fall.

The name dates to 1881 in SSA records and has been present in every decade since, a long, quiet history similar to Sebastian's fellow German-origin name Oliver, though without Oliver's recent acceleration.

Johann Sebastian Bach anchors the name to a very different era and field than its other famous bearers — Formula One's Sebastian Vettel, actor Rowan Atkinson (born Rowan Sebastian Atkinson), and former Austrian chancellor Sebastian Kurz — a spread across three centuries and several countries that may help explain why the name has stayed steady rather than tracking any single trend.

jack.text:
Jack's current #15 ranking sits well below its actual historical peak: 12,802 births in 1927, nearly a century before this data point. But the recent trend line is nearly flat — 8,434 births in 2024 is only 4% below the count from ten years earlier, a rare case in this batch of a name that has stopped declining rather than one still falling.

It's been recorded since 1880 and its most recent local high point, rank #11, came as recently as 2021, suggesting the long post-1920s decline may have leveled off rather than continuing indefinitely, unlike Ava's still-steep 45% ten-year drop.

The famous-bearer list — Jack London, Jack Kerouac, Jack Lemmon, Jack Kilby — leans toward American writers and inventors across the 20th century, a different profile from a name like Liam or Mateo whose namesakes are almost entirely contemporary athletes and entertainers, fitting a name whose core popularity long predates its current famous bearers.

daniel.text:
Daniel peaked in 1985 at 38,564 births — more than four times its current count — and the name has been declining steadily since, down 40% over just the past decade to 8,391 in 2024, the second-steepest ten-year percentage drop in this batch, behind only Ava's 45%.

It's been recorded since 1880 and has held a top-20 rank continuously for most of the past several decades, meaning its current #16 position, while down from a 1985 rank of #5, still represents remarkable staying power for a name this far past its peak.

Its famous-bearer list spans jazz (Louis Armstrong, whose middle name was Daniel), literature (Daniel Defoe), and film (Daniel Radcliffe, Daniel Craig) — a name that has apparently supplied recognizable public figures in every generation since the 1900s without needing a fresh cultural spike to stay in circulation, even as its raw birth numbers fall.

samuel.text:
Samuel's best-ever rank, #17, was already achieved in 1880 — the very first year the SSA data covers — meaning by the time this dataset starts recording, the name had already peaked positionally and everything since has been a name holding on rather than climbing. Its raw count peaked much later, 14,813 births in 2001, but even that high point never matched the name's relative dominance from 1880.

Today's 8,310 births in 2024 is down 25% from a decade earlier, a decline shared with several long-standing names in this range rather than anything specific to Samuel.

The famous-bearer list runs almost entirely through 18th- and 19th-century letters — lexicographer Samuel Johnson, poet Samuel Taylor Coleridge, telegraph inventor Samuel Morse — with Mark Twain (born Samuel Clemens) as the closest thing to a household name. That's a narrower, more literary cluster than most names this size carry, most of them born well before the 20th century.

michael.text:
Michael's scale dwarfs almost everything else in this range: 4,440,391 total US births since 1880, and it was the #1 boys' name for a long stretch through the mid-1950s, peaking at 92,786 births in a single year, 1957 — a figure that puts it in the same historical tier as James and William from the top-25 batch.

The drop-off since has been sharp by comparison: 8,189 births in 2024, down 47% from ten years prior, one of the steeper declines among the long-established names covered so far. Even so, #18 nationally is a remarkable landing spot for a name whose peak was nearly six figures in a single year.

Michael Jackson, Michael Jordan, and Michael Faraday cover music, sport, and science across three different centuries, which is typical of a name this old — its famous-bearer list reads less like a snapshot of one generation and more like a running tally across the whole 20th century.

asher.text:
Asher is still on its way up: an 87% rise over the past decade brought it to its highest-ever rank, #20, in 2022, and 2024's count of 8,123 sits only slightly below that peak of 8,410 — a name that hasn't yet shown any sign of turning over.

Its history in the data has real gaps: the decades-active list skips the 1900s entirely, meaning fewer than five Asher births were recorded in the US in that decade, before the name picked back up in the 1910s and has appeared in every decade since — an unusually specific dormant stretch for a name with roots this old (first recorded in 1880).

Its famous-bearer list is a mix of the historical and the very recent — 19th-century painter Asher Brown Durand, playwright Arthur Miller (born Asher Miller), and Disney Channel actor Asher Angel — which, unlike Michael's steady multi-century presence, looks more like a name that went quiet for most of its history and only recently found an audience.

ethan.text:
Ethan shows a pattern worth flagging because it recurs across several names in this range: its raw count peaked in 2004 at 22,210 births, but its best-ever rank, #2, didn't arrive until 2009 — five years after the count itself started falling. A name's rank can keep climbing even as its own numbers shrink, if its competitors are shrinking faster.

By 2024 that rank has slid to #19, with 8,170 births, down 48% from a decade earlier — one of the steeper ten-year declines among boys' names in this range, alongside Michael's.

Its famous-bearer list skews almost entirely contemporary, tilted toward European football (Ethan Ampadu, Ethan Nwaneri) and American film (Ethan Hawke, Ethan Suplee), a spread that contrasts with older names like Samuel or Michael whose namesakes reach back centuries — reflecting how recently Ethan actually built its popularity, first entering the data only in 1882.

sofia.text:
Sofia — this spelling, distinct from "Sophia" — is a useful contrast to its more common cousin: both are declining in raw count, but Sofia just reached its best-ever national rank, #10, in 2024, even as its count fell 16% over the decade to 8,094. Like Amelia in the top-25 batch, it's benefiting from the general spreading-out of the naming pool rather than any growth of its own.

It first appears in SSA records in 1881, only a year after Sophia, and the two spellings have tracked each other loosely ever since without ever fully merging into one dominant form.

Sofia Loren, Sofia Coppola, and Sofia Carson span film across nearly a century, along with the enrichment data's cross-listing of Sophia Loren under this shorter spelling — a reminder that spelling variants of the same name often share famous bearers in ways strict alphabetical splitting doesn't fully capture.

hudson.text:
At 7,990 births, Hudson's 2024 count is its best yet, a 52% jump over the past decade that's brought it to #22 nationally — one of the more recent entrants to this range of the chart, with barely two famous bearers on record compared to the five-deep lists most established names carry.

The name technically dates to 1880 in SSA data, but its enrichment data only surfaces two notable namesakes: blues musician Lead Belly, born Huddie Ledbetter — an indirect connection at best — and actor Hudson Williams, born 2001, close in age to the current wave of babies given the name. That thinness in cultural reference points is unusual for a name climbing this fast; most rising names in this range (Asher, Luca, Elias) carry a longer or more varied list of namesakes even while newer to popularity.

Hudson reads more like a place-name-turned-first-name — after the river, most likely — than a name tied to any individual, which may explain why its rise hasn't produced the kind of namesake cluster that names like Ethan or Owen have.

john.text:
John's total of 5,196,210 births since 1880 edges out Michael's and even James's from the top-25 batch, and like Samuel and William before it, its best-ever rank — #1 — was already locked in by 1880, the first year this dataset covers. Its single biggest year came later, 1947, with 88,321 births.

Today it sits at #21 with 8,047 births in 2024, down 25% over the decade — the same percentage decline as Samuel, though John's much larger historical base means the absolute drop represents a bigger swing in real terms.

The famous-bearer list spans philosophy (John Locke), literature (J. R. R. Tolkien, born John Ronald Reuel Tolkien), and politics (John F. Kennedy, John Adams) across four centuries — a name whose cultural weight was already fully established well before the 20th-century birth boom that produced its highest single-year count.

luca.text:
Luca is the fastest-growing name in this batch by a wide margin: 245% higher than a decade earlier, with both its raw count and its rank hitting new highs in the same year, 2024 — 7,959 births, its best ever, at #23 nationally, with no sign yet of a peak behind it.

Its history is unusually broken up: first recorded in 1915, with activity that then skips the 1930s and 1950s entirely — two full decades with fewer than five US births — before resuming and eventually taking off in the 2010s and 2020s. Few names in this range show that kind of on-again, off-again presence across a century of data.

Its famous bearers lean heavily Italian and historical — Renaissance mathematician Luca Pacioli, painter Luca Signorelli — alongside recent figures like director Luca Guadagnino and footballer Luca Toni, a spread that tracks the name's Italian origin more closely than most of its English-origin neighbors in this batch.

dylan.text:
Dylan is one of the youngest names in this batch by data history: it first appears in US birth records only in 1953, decades later than the 1880 starting point most names in this range share. Its count peaked in 2001 at 16,497, but its best-ever rank, #19, wasn't reached until 2003 — the same lagged pattern seen in Ethan.

By 2024 its rank had slipped to #28, with 7,464 births — 28% below where it stood a decade earlier, a milder decline than Ethan's or Michael's but still a clear retreat from its early-2000s high.

Its famous-bearer list skews almost entirely toward film and streaming — Dylan O'Brien, Dylan Minnette, Jack Dylan Grazer — young actors rather than an older cultural reference, consistent with a name whose entire US popularity has unfolded within living memory rather than across generations.

leo.text:
Leo has already cooled from a very recent high: its rank peaked at #18 in 2023, just one year before this data ends, and by 2024 it had slipped to #24 even though the raw count, 7,793, is still close to its 2022 peak of 8,290. A 96% rise over the decade is one of the larger gains in this batch, but the rank slippage suggests the climb may already be leveling off.

The name has been recorded since 1880, giving it a longer paper trail than its recent surge might suggest, similar in shape to Asher's pattern of old roots and a recent breakout.

Its famous-bearer list is dominated by French cultural figures under the accented spelling Léo — composer Léo Delibes, singer Johnny Hallyday (born Jean-Philippe Léo Smet) — pointing to a European namesake pool quite different from the largely American or British lists attached to names like Hudson or Owen.

elias.text:
Elias is still climbing without any sign of a turn: both its count and its rank hit new highs in the same year, 2024 — 7,653 births at #25 nationally, 102% higher than a decade earlier. Unlike Leo or Owen, whose rank has already started pulling back from a recent peak, Elias hasn't yet shown that kind of reversal.

SSA records go back to 1880 for this name, more than a century of quiet background presence before this recent acceleration.

Its famous-bearer list is unusually cross-disciplinary for a name this size — Walt Disney (born Walter Elias Disney), Nobel-winning writer Elias Canetti, 12th-century Persian poet Nizami Ganjavi (born Elyas), and Brazilian former president Michel Temer (born Michel Miguel Elias Temer Lulia) — a spread across entertainment, literature, poetry, and politics that most similarly-sized names don't match.

camila.text:
Camila has held essentially the same rank, #11, since its 2020 peak — 8,164 births that year against 7,608 in 2024, a modest pullback in count but no real change in position, unlike several names in this batch whose rank has already dropped several places from its high point.

The name entered SSA records in 1914 and has grown 46% over the past decade, a steady climb rather than a sudden spike, with no gaps in its decades-active history since.

Its famous-bearer list is heavily contemporary and entertainment-driven — singer Camila Cabello, actor Camila Mendes, model Camila Morrone — almost entirely people born in the 1990s, a narrower generational cluster than names like Elias or John whose namesakes span centuries.

owen.text:
Owen's rank has fallen further and faster than its raw numbers alone would suggest: it peaked at #18 in 2022 but had dropped to #26 by 2024, an eight-place slide in just two years, even though the count decline over the full decade is a comparatively mild 17%. That gap between a sharp recent rank drop and a gentler long-term count trend is unusual in this batch.

The name shows up in every decade of SSA data since 1880, a long and steady history before its 2016 peak of 10,302 births.

Its famous-bearer list mixes science (Nobel physicist Owen Willans Richardson, Owen Chamberlain) with entertainment (Owen Wilson) and sport (Owen Hargreaves) — a broad spread that doesn't cluster around any single field the way Camila's or Dylan's namesake lists do.

alexander.text:
Alexander's slide is one of the sharpest of any established name in this range — down 51% over the past decade — after dropping from a peak position of #4, its best ever, held in 2009, all the way to #27 by 2024. Its raw-count peak came earlier still, 20,529 births in 1993, meaning the name has now been declining in some form for roughly three decades.

It's been recorded since 1880 and carries a total of 733,348 US births, a large historical base for a name now well outside the top 20.

The famous-bearer list is dense with 19th-century scientists and scholars — Alexander Graham Bell, Alexander von Humboldt, Alexander Fleming — a concentration of invention and discovery that few other names in this batch match, though none of it appears to have slowed the name's recent slide.

harper.text:
Harper is one of the youngest names in this entire batch by history: it first appears in SSA data only in 1971, more than a century after most of its neighbors here, and its enrichment data lists exactly one famous bearer — novelist Harper Lee, born Nelle Harper Lee in 1926, whose fame predates the name's use as a first name by decades.

Its rank peaked at #9 in 2018, and by 2024 it had eased to #12 with 7,370 births, down 23% over the decade — a milder decline than Alexander's or Michael's, consistent with a name still relatively early in its adoption cycle rather than one fading from a much older peak.

That combination — a very short data history, a single strong namesake, and a comparatively gentle decline — makes Harper's trajectory look less like the long rise-and-fall arcs of Michael or John and more like a recent cultural pick that's still finding its ceiling.

santiago.text:
Santiago set new highs in both count and rank in the same year, 2024 — 7,407 births at #29 nationally, 116% higher than ten years earlier — with no indication yet of the kind of pullback already visible in Leo or Owen.

SSA records for this name stretch back to 1880, a long quiet history before this recent climb, similar in shape to Elias and Asher: old roots, recent breakout.

Its famous-bearer list is dense with Spanish-language achievement across very different fields — neuroscientist Santiago Ramón y Cajal, architect Santiago Calatrava, footballer Federico Valverde (whose full name includes Santiago) — a cluster of intellectual and athletic figures that fits the name's Spanish origin more tightly than most of its English-origin neighbors in this batch manage with theirs.

julian.text:
Julian is at its best-ever rank right now: #30 in 2024, exactly matching its peak, with a birth count that's held nearly flat over the past decade — down just 4% — one of the smallest ten-year swings covered in this batch.

This name appears in every US decade of data from 1880 onward, and its raw-count peak came in 2017 at 8,451 births — a gentle decline since, to 7,368 in 2024, rather than any sharp drop.

The famous-bearer list runs from 19th-century polish nobility-adjacent naming through to WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange and Nobel physicist Julian Schwinger — a spread across politics, science, and literature (Julian Barnes) that doesn't lean toward any single decade the way Camila's or Dylan's lists do.

david.text:
David's scale places it among the largest names in this entire dataset: 3,682,683 total US births since 1880, with a single-year peak of 86,301 in 1955. Its best-ever rank, #1, came five years later in 1960 — the same lagged pattern seen in Ethan and Dylan, where a name's positional peak trails its raw-count peak.

By 2024 its rank had dropped to #31, with 7,317 births — 40% below where it stood a decade earlier, a steeper decline than John's or Samuel's despite a broadly similar historical arc.

Its famous-bearer list spans philosophy (David Hume), mathematics (David Hilbert), and politics (David Cameron, Dwight D. Eisenhower's full name includes David) across four centuries, a breadth that puts it in the same historical tier as John or Michael even though its current rank sits noticeably lower than either.

joseph.text:
Joseph shows the widest gap in this batch between when its rank peaked and when its raw count peaked: rank hit #5 all the way back in 1912, but the actual count didn't reach its high of 32,748 until 1956 — a 44-year lag, far longer than the four-or-five-year gaps seen in Ethan or David, meaning Joseph was proportionally more dominant among a much smaller pool of names in 1912 than it ever was at its later numerical peak.

Total births since 1880 run to 2,672,746. In 2024 it counted 7,223 births, 41% fewer than a decade earlier, landing it at #32 nationally.

The famous-bearer list bridges entertainment and politics unusually directly — Michael Jackson (born Michael Joseph Jackson), Joe Biden (born Joseph Robinette Biden), Pope Benedict XVI (born Joseph Ratzinger) — three very different kinds of public figures who all carry Joseph as a given rather than middle name.

luna.text:
Luna's rise is one of the sharpest in this batch: a 205% increase over the past decade, though its best-ever rank, #10, was reached in 2022 and has already eased to #13 by 2024 — a recent pullback similar to Leo's and Owen's, following a period of very fast growth.

Unusually for a name of Latin origin with data going back to 1880, its only listed famous bearer is fictional: Luna Lovegood, from the Harry Potter series, whose Wikidata "born" year of 1981 refers to the character's story timeline rather than a real person. That's a different kind of namesake than any other entry in this batch carries.

Whether that fictional association is driving the name's recent surge isn't something the birth data alone can confirm, but Luna's growth curve — old roots, a long quiet period, then a sudden climb — matches the shape of several other recently-popular names here, like Asher and Santiago.

eleanor.text:
Eleanor's raw count actually peaked back in 1920 at 8,497 births. A 91% climb over the last ten years — among the larger gains in this batch — still hasn't been enough to push 2024's count of 7,127 past that century-old high. It's a similar shape to Evelyn's story in the top-25 batch: an early-20th-century peak, a long quiet stretch, and a modern recovery that's real but not yet complete.

Its rank, unlike its count, has already reached a new high — #14 in 2023 — since the smaller pool of competing names today means fewer births are needed to hold a strong position than in 1920.

The famous-bearer list carries unusual political and literary weight: Eleanor Roosevelt, Margaret Atwood (born Margaret Eleanor Atwood), and medieval queen Eleanor of Aquitaine span eight centuries, a range matched by few other names in this batch.

matthew.text:
Matthew shows this batch's longest lag between a raw-count peak and a rank peak: it peaked at 50,208 births in 1983 but didn't reach its best-ever rank, #2, until 1995 — twelve years later, even longer than Joseph's 44-year gap in absolute terms is proportionally shorter given Matthew's peak came in living memory rather than a century ago.

By 2024 it had fallen to 7,078 births, 45% below its count a decade prior, landing it at #33 nationally — a steeper decline than John's or Samuel's, closer to Michael's or Ethan's pace.

Its famous-bearer list leans heavily toward film and music from the past several decades — Matt Damon, Matthew McConaughey, Matthew Perry, plus Sting (born Gordon Matthew Thomas Sumner) — a modern, entertainment-heavy cluster that contrasts with the centuries-spanning lists attached to older names like David or John.

logan.text:
Logan has the steepest ten-year decline in this entire batch: down 54% since a decade ago, to 6,267 births in 2024, dropping it to #46 — well below most other names covered here. Its raw count peaked earlier, in 2007 at 15,330, and its best-ever rank, #5, came a full decade later in 2017, the same delayed-rank pattern seen in Ethan and David, before the recent sharp fall.

This name has appeared in every decade of US data since 1880, a long history before its 21st-century surge and subsequent retreat.

The famous-bearer list mixes fiction and reality in an unusual way: the Marvel character Wolverine (real name Logan, per the enrichment data's "born" field of 1832) sits alongside YouTuber Logan Paul and Formula One's Logan Sargeant — a spread from 19th-century comic-book backstory to 21st-century internet fame that no other name in this batch quite matches.

luke.text:
Luke is one of the few names in this batch where the raw-count peak and the rank peak landed in exactly the same year: 2014, both times — a cleaner, simultaneous high point than the multi-year lags seen in Ethan, David, or Matthew.

Since then it's fallen to #34 with 7,039 births in 2024, down 33% over the decade, a decline in the middle of this batch's range — steeper than Julian's near-flat trend but milder than Logan's steep drop.

Its most culturally prominent association carries no real birth year at all: Luke Skywalker's enrichment entry lists "born: null," a fictional character whose influence on the name's popularity can't be measured the same way as a real namesake. The name's other bearers — footballer Luke Shaw, actors Luke Perry and Luke Evans — are all real, contemporary figures rather than the older names one might expect for something this established.

avery.text:
Avery's data starts in 1890, a decade later than most of its neighbors in this batch but well before recent arrivals like Dylan (1953) or Harper (1971).

Its rank peaked at #12 in 2013, one year ahead of its raw-count peak of 9,578 in 2014 — the peak-then-count pattern seen in a few other names here, just reversed in order. By 2024 its count had dropped to 5,632, a 41% decline over ten years that left it at #31 — one of the steeper drops in this batch alongside David's and Joseph's.

Its famous-bearer list is entirely contemporary and entertainment-adjacent — actors Bella Thorne and Troian Bellisario, singer Grace VanderWaal — young public figures rather than any older reference point, fitting a name whose current form of popularity is a relatively recent development despite its longer data history.
